title: 5 insightful analyst questions from Microsoft’s Q3 earnings call - TradingView
content: Microsoft’s third quarter saw positive market reaction as revenue and non-GAAP earnings per share surpassed Wall Street expectations. Management credited widespread adoption of its cloud and AI offerings—particularly Copilot and Foundry—for this performance, pointing to rapid growth in enterprise demand and expanded use cases across commercial and consumer segments. CEO Satya Nadella highlighted that “automated tasks have nearly doubled since July,” with customer momentum translating into larger Copilot deployments and higher usage-based revenue. While we enjoy listening to the management’s commentary, our favorite part of earnings calls is the analyst questions. Those are unscripted and can often highlight topics that management teams would rather avoid or topics where the answer is complicated. Here is what has caught our attention. Our top 5 analyst questions from Microsoft’s Q3 earnings call Adam Wood (Morgan Stanley) asked about the main drivers of long-term returns, focusing on infrastructure utilization versus monetizing more product layers. CEO Satya Nadella replied that margin improvements will come from both more efficient infrastructure and expanding monetization across products. Karl Keirstead (UBS) inquired about the drivers behind Azure’s projected growth. CFO Amy Hood explained that recent gains stem from engineering-driven efficiency, Foundry allocation, and higher token pricing, but noted variability in supply and usage-based pricing. Mark Moerdler (Bernstein Research) questioned the mix of enterprise versus digitally native AI workloads. Nadella emphasized growing breadth of enterprise adoption, with examples from sectors like manufacturing and finance, and noted that enterprise-scale workloads are becoming the norm. Brent Thill (Jefferies) asked if Microsoft can sustain high operating margins alongside rapid revenue growth. Hood responded that operational excellence, efficiency, and integrated product delivery are key to maintaining profitability. Brad Reback (Stifel) probed the speed of adoption for usage-based billing outside of coding. Nadella acknowledged it will be faster in developer tools, while enterprise productivity solutions will require more gradual customer education and sales efforts. Looking ahead, the StockStory team will closely monitor (1) continued enterprise adoption and deployment scale of Copilot and Foundry, (2) incremental gains in cloud infrastructure efficiency and capacity expansion, and (3) the pace of migration from per-seat to usage-based billing across Microsoft’s product suite. Updates on customer demand for new AI models and supply chain progress for data center components will also be critical to watch. title: Estée Lauder Expands Microsoft AI Partnership As It Targets Productivity, Personalized Experiences - TradingView
content: The Estée Lauder Companies (EL) announced a strategic partnership with Microsoft (MSFT) on Friday to strengthen its cloud and data infrastructure and support the responsible adoption of AI across its business. “Our partnership with Microsoft, in addition to the other strategic partners in our One Operating Ecosystem, is powering our teams with the capabilities to ultimately deliver more relevant, personalized experiences that meet consumers’ evolving needs,” said Brian Franz, chief technology and transformation officer at Estée Lauder. EL shares traded 2.5% lower, and MSFT shares traded 1.5% lower at the time of writing. Microsoft Copilot Reaches More Than 14,000 Employees Estée Lauder has expanded Microsoft Copilot across its global office-based workforce, reaching more than 14,000 employees. The partnership focuses on three strategic priorities: New Capabilities & Growth, Decision Intelligence, and Productivity & Automation. The company is also experimenting with productivity agents and embedding AI into role-specific workflows while automating repetitive manual tasks. Estée Lauder said these tools are intended to help employees focus on strategy, innovation, and higher-value decision-making. Partnership Targets Data, Consumer Insights, Product Development The collaboration will advance Estée Lauder’s Unified Data Platform, which connects data across brands, regions, channels and functions. The company said the platform is designed to reduce duplication, enable reusable data products and improve access to data-driven insights. The company is also investing in a Unified Consumer Data Platform to deepen its understanding of consumer needs and preferences. Combined with connected product data, the platform is designed to support personalized experiences from product discovery to purchase and inform product innovation, drawing on the company’s 80 years of consumer understanding and beauty expertise. Separately, Estée Lauder is developing a connected, AI-powered workflow across product design, validation and manufacturing. The initiative aims to help teams make faster, more coordinated decisions and move products from idea to launch more efficiently. Franz said the partnership’s enhanced capabilities would help Estée Lauder “drive sustainable growth, improve productivity, and support margin expansion,” while creating capacity for reinvestment. Microsoft Executive Vice President and Chief Revenue Officer Deb Cupp said the collaboration would help turn insights into action at scale, from empowering employees to modernizing product development and delivering more meaningful consumer experiences. The partnership supports Estée Lauder’s Beauty Reimagined strategy and forms part of its One Operating Ecosystem. title: Microsoft Is Borrowing $25 Billion for AI, Its First Bond Sale Since 2017 - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Microsoft holds more cash than most countries, yet it just lined up to borrow from bond markets for the first time in nearly a decade. The reason reveals something uncomfortable about what AI is actually costing the world's most creditworthy… On October 29, 2026, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) priced $25 billion of senior unsecured bonds. It was the company’s first U.S. dollar bond sale since 2017, the year it raised $17 billion. Orders topped out at $115 billion, or 4.6 times the deal size. The stock hardly moved. Shares closed that day at $530.14, down 0.16%, for a market value of $3.94 trillion. That came after a 4.1% after-hours jump to $552.55 on October 28, which faded. Microsoft (MSFT) The Least Magnificent of the Mag 7 - Time To Sell? Bond buyers accepted a premium for rare AAA debt from the strongest borrower in corporate America, while stock buyers were looking at a company whose spending is growing faster than its cash. Microsoft holds more cash than long-term debt, so the real question is why it chose to borrow. Once the bonds were priced, the debt was committed. The deal has 10 tranches, meaning separate bonds that mature at different dates, running from two years to 40 years. The bond due 2066 priced at 1.05 percentage points over Treasuries. That was as much as 0.3 points tighter than initial guidance, so investors accepted a smaller premium than first offered. How the money gets spent is only stated intent. Microsoft listed general corporate purposes, including capital expenditures and share buybacks. So the bonds help pay for an AI-driven build, but none of the money is specifically set aside for AI. The size and coupon of each tranche had not been widely reported as of October 30, 2026. On the October 28 earnings call, CFO Amy Hood spoke. She said Microsoft has “lots of options to be able to tap the financing markets when they make sense and they’re attractive.” Before the deal, Microsoft had $64.5 billion of cash and short-term investments and $31.1 billion of long-term debt. The reason it borrowed anyway shows up in the fiscal first quarter. Capital spending, including finance leases, was $45.2 billion, and cash paid for property and equipment was $39.4 billion. A finance lease gets recorded like a purchase. It is a long-term rental of data center capacity, which is why those two numbers differ. Microsoft now expects about $175 billion of capex for calendar 2026, compared with $190 billion in April. Most of that difference comes from an accounting change that shifts more leases to operating leases, and those sit outside capex. Borrowing at AAA rates lets Microsoft keep its cash for buybacks and construction while spending runs ahead of what the business brings in. It also locks in 40-year money while lenders are eager to supply it. The 2066 bond priced tighter than Alphabet’s (NASDAQ:GOOG, NASDAQ:GOOGL) 40-year bond, which trades near 1.33 points over Treasuries. Alphabet sold $25 billion of bonds on August 6. Five-year credit default swaps measure the yearly cost of insuring a company’s debt against default. Microsoft’s sit at about 54 basis points, compared with 116 for Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and 275 for Oracle (NYSE:ORCL). Lenders therefore see paying for Oracle’s expansion as much riskier than paying for Microsoft’s. Microsoft was a latecomer to the borrowing wave. Hyperscalers and data center developers have issued more than $313 billion of investment-grade bonds globally in 2026, and the proceeds flow well beyond the chipmakers to the power, cooling, and networking suppliers behind each facility (we profiled seven of those winners in a free report you can grab here). Brett Kozlowski of GW&K called the timing “opportunistic”. Still, the fact that Microsoft borrowed at all shows that even the strongest balance sheet now wants outside money for this cycle. Revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion. Azure grew 48% in constant currency, ahead of Microsoft’s own 44% to 45% forecast, and management said customer demand continued to exceed available supply. The falling stock reflects a fair worry about spending, since Microsoft expects second-quarter capex of over $50 billion. That risk grows. It grows further if AI demand slows while borrowed money funds buybacks, or if repeated bond sales put pressure on the AAA rating. The test is the fiscal second-quarter earnings report. Microsoft guided for Azure growth of 49 to 50% in constant currency. The case for the stock weakens. If Azure falls short of that range while capex tops $50 billion, a close below the October 29 low of $519.56 would signal market agreement. While Alphabet's (GOOGL) stock is getting crushed on Thursday after earnings, Microsoft (MSFT) is largely getting a pass. Another way of saying it: Microsoft shares aren't significantly trading down in sympathy. And there is one simple reason why this is the case. Microsoft's quarter is being seen as one of higher-than-expected growth that is sustainable, while Alphabet's quarter was sluggish and hinted at slowing growth rates in coming quarters. Microsoft's Azure sales growth came in about 300 basis points above analyst estimates. Overall sales for the important cloud business grew 48%, excluding currency fluctuations. Execs guided to 49% to 50% Azure sales growth in the current quarter, ahead of consensus estimates by four percentage points. The company's capex came in about $5 billion below estimates, and other parts of the business showed sales upside. Sales and earnings for the quarter came in ahead of analyst forecasts. "Net/net, these results increase our confidence in the company's ability to sustain mid/upper-teens revenue growth and that strong cost of goods sold/expense operational efficiencies should be supportive of expanding operating margins," said stifel analyst Brad Reback. Alphabet shares tanked 12% after a third quarter that could best be characterized as a letdown, both on its own and versus Microsoft. content: Intel heads into its quarterly earnings report carrying a fresh foundry wound, a slide in Big Tech results, and analysts who think the stock is still too expensive. Whether management can name real outside customers tonight may determine if the… A foundry setback and a rough night for Big Tech earnings are piling pressure on Intel (NASDAQ:INTC | INTC Price Prediction) hours before its own quarterly report. Intel stock is at $92.04, down 4% in recent trading. The slide adds to a 20% drop over the past month, which followed a powerful run earlier in the year. Intel’s decline is steeper than its sector’s. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH), a fund concentrated in chipmakers, is at $561.62, down 1.1%. At the same time, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is at $714.93, down 1.5%, falling harder than the chip fund as Big Tech earnings weigh on large-cap stocks. The latest blow landed on October 29, when Elon Musk’s Terafab chip initiative confirmed it’s in active discussions with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing about a dedicated fabrication plant to supply chips for Musk’s companies. That undermines Intel’s earlier positioning as a central foundry partner for the project. Big outside customers matter because Intel Foundry is still losing money. In Q2 2026, Intel Foundry’s revenue rose 31% to $5.76 billion, while the unit ran a $2.1 billion quarterly operating loss. Intel reports Q3 2026 results after the closing bell, a date the company has confirmed. Bernstein modeled Intel’s Q4 2026 revenue below Street consensus, citing PC market weakness and estimating third-quarter PC shipments were down 20% to 22% year over year. Wedbush noted that Taiwan Semiconductor may raise prices on its Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate (CoWoS) advanced packaging by 10% to 20%, which the firm views as a renewed supply chain constraint and a reduced competitive opportunity for Intel. JPMorgan, which recently upgraded Intel to Neutral, carries an $85 price target that sits below the current share price. After the close on October 28, Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) reported Q3 2026 revenue of $127.58 billion, up 24.6% year over year and slightly missing expectations. Alphabet stock is at $284.82, down 12%. The company earned $2.12 per share, missing the $2.97 consensus, after an $8.7 billion loss on equity securities that Alphabet disclosed reduced diluted earnings by $0.55 per share. Without that one-time hit, Alphabet’s quarter centered on AI demand. Google Cloud revenue jumped 103% to $30.71 billion, helped by sales of its custom tensor processing unit (TPU) systems, and CEO Sundar Pichai said, “We’re also seeing strong demand for our TPU systems across a wide range of customers.” Spending is the catch: Alphabet’s capital expenditures reached $51.36 billion and its free cash flow turned negative at $9.07 billion, renewing worries about AI infrastructure costs (we covered seven suppliers supporting that expansion, from power to cooling, in a free report). Meanwhile, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) stock is at $524.40, down 1%. Microsoft’s Q1 FY2027 revenue rose 18.8% to $92.28 billion, and its adjusted earnings of $4.89 per share beat the $4.72 consensus. For Intel, the sore spot is the PC outlook, since Microsoft guided its Windows original equipment manufacturer (OEM) and devices revenue to decline by a percentage in the mid-30s in Q2 FY2027. Chip stocks including Intel declined on Samsung’s profit miss and the heavy capital spending disclosed by Microsoft and Alphabet. That combination leaves Intel absorbing both AI spending worries and a weaker PC backdrop. Intel designs and manufactures its own chips, from Xeon server processors to Core Ultra PC chips, and wants to sell factory capacity on its 18A process to outside customers. Google runs search, YouTube and a fast-growing cloud on TPU silicon it designs in-house for its AI workloads. Microsoft rents out Azure capacity built on third-party graphics processing units and, increasingly, its own chip designs, and it’s a potential but unconfirmed Intel foundry customer. In this trio, Intel is the supplier hoping the other two turn into buyers. When Intel reports after the close, the key question is whether management can name new outside foundry customers. Intel’s Q2 2026 results offer some encouragement, with revenue growing 25.4% to $16.13 billion and data center and AI sales rising 59%. The AI boom is reshaping cloud computing, creating opportunities for both specialized AI infrastructure providers and established technology giants. Two companies at the focus of this transformation are CoreWeave, Inc. CRWV and Microsoft Corporation MSFT. Per a report from Fortune Business Insights, the global cloud AI market size is anticipated to go from $133.4 billion in 2026 to $780.6 billion by 2034 at a CAGR of 23.8%. CoreWeave offers specialized cloud infrastructure built around high-performance GPUs, while Microsoft combines its Azure cloud platform with enterprise software, AI models and products such as Microsoft 365 Copilot. Both companies are poised to benefit from growing AI workloads, but their investment cases differ considerably. The key question for investors is which stock offers greater upside potential from its current valuation. CoreWeave could deliver stronger percentage gains if AI infrastructure demand and profitability exceed expectations. Microsoft, however, offers a more diversified business, established cash generation and broader opportunities to monetize AI. Microsoft delivered a strong first quarter of fiscal 2027, with revenue up 19% year over year to $92.3 billion, operating income up 21% to $45.9 billion, Azure revenue rising 48% and Microsoft Cloud revenue growing 30% to $63.9 billion. Accelerating Microsoft Cloud growth, robust Azure demand and expanding commercial commitments highlight the company's ability to capitalize on rising enterprise investment in AI and cloud infrastructure. Its diversified revenue streams provide a financial cushion that a specialized infrastructure provider does not have. The company introduced major Copilot updates, integrating Chat, Cowork, Autopilot and Code into a unified experience, while new AI models and agentic development tools are expanding applications in coding, security and enterprise automation. Microsoft is also strengthening AI governance, data management and contextual intelligence through tools such as Microsoft Purview, Fabric and Microsoft IQ. Commercial remaining performance obligation (RPO) increased 73%, representing a robust pipeline of contracted future business. Cloud infrastructure remains a key growth driver, backed by strong AI demand, Foundry adoption and infrastructure efficiencies. Microsoft added 24 data centers globally and is optimizing capacity to improve throughput and costs. Enterprise AI adoption continues to broaden across industries, including healthcare, financial services and supply chains, while Dynamics 365 and LinkedIn are also benefiting from AI integration. Microsoft Corporation price-consensus-chart | Microsoft Corporation Quote For the second quarter of fiscal 2027, Microsoft expects revenue of $96-$97.1 billion, with Azure growth projected at 49-50%. Capital expenditures are expected to exceed $50 billion as the company expands AI infrastructure to address demand that continues to outpace supply. Despite heavy investments, Microsoft is prioritizing infrastructure efficiency, cost management and strong operating margins to improve returns. It returned $10.2 billion to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases during the fiscal first quarter. However, declining Windows OEM and Devices revenue, modest weakness in Xbox content and services, and the lumpsum investment requirements associated with AI infrastructure remain important factors for investors to monitor. Microsoft also faces challenges in its consumer segment, with Windows OEM revenue declining 22% amid inventory and PC demand pressures, although Bing, Edge and Xbox reported positive engagement trends. CoreWeave continues to expand its AI cloud platform, adding 500 MW of active power capacity in the second quarter to reach 1.5 GW, with contracted power increasing to 4.2 GW. The company is expanding into Asia-Pacific and targeting more than 8 GW of active power capacity by 2030. It recently expanded its global AI cloud platform, bringing most of its planned 22.5 MW of IT capacity online at a Copenhagen data center while extending its network into the Middle East and Asia Pacific. The expansion could strengthen its competitive position amid rising global AI demand. Platform innovations across training, inference and managed services are broadening its capabilities, with managed inference ARR growing from $1 million to more than $100 million since launch. Management expects this business to reach at least $250 million in ARR by year-end. Strong customer demand, premium pricing and supply-chain efficiencies are supporting margin expansion despite intensifying competition. CoreWeave is also capitalizing on legacy GPU infrastructure through renewals and shorter-duration contracts, while expanding its managed inference offerings. Its focus on reliability, security and flexible infrastructure helps differentiate its platform across a growing range of AI workloads. CoreWeave strengthened its financial flexibility through debt and equity financing, raising more than $18 billion and reducing its average debt cost by 300 basis points. Although heavy investment and financing requirements remain key risks, the company expects sustained AI demand and capacity expansion to drive future growth. However, CoreWeave faces risks from heavy capital spending, rising financing costs and customer concentration. Rising infrastructure investments pushed capital expenditures to $9.4 billion in the second quarter, with full-year guidance raised to $35-$39 billion, increasing reliance on debt, equity and other funding sources. Customer concentration remains another concern, as three customers accounted for 72% of second-quarter revenue, while two customers each represented 32% of accounts receivable. Although CoreWeave is expanding into new industries and lowering borrowing costs, its substantial funding needs and dependence on a few major customers remain key risks. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for CRWV's earnings for the current year has been revised downward over the past 60 days. Both CRWV and MSFT at present carry a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). Its rapid revenue growth and large backlog could drive significant share-price appreciation if it executes successfully, improves operating profitability and manages its debt burden. However, financing requirements, execution delays and the risk of shareholder dilution make it a higher-risk investment. MSFT offers a broader way to participate in AI adoption. Azure's strong growth, enterprise software ecosystem and profitability provide multiple avenues for monetization. Its substantial capital spending remains a risk, but its diversified operations offer greater resilience. CRWV may offer greater percentage upside for risk-tolerant, long-term investors if growth translates into sustainable cash flow, while MSFT is better suited to investors seeking stable earnings, diversification and lower risk. title: Alphabet tanks nearly 13% for worst day ever, losing $500 billion in value - CNBC
content:
Alphabet shares plunged the most since Google went public in 2004, dropping 13% on Thursday, wiping out roughly $500 billion in market cap. In its earnings announcement late Wednesday, Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion for the third quarter, compared to the $2.7 billion analysts expected. The Google parent maintained its full year capital expenditure guidance of between $195 billion and $205 billion. Microsoft, meanwhile, traded largely flat as investors focused on the tech giants’ latest spending and free cash flow numbers in the third-quarter earnings report. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, which was 30% higher than a year ago, but below analyst projections of $50.67 billion. Free cash flow fell 27% to $18.63 billion but remained positive. The earnings reports come as investors scrutinize AI spending plans of tech companies and are focusing on the returns on those investments. “Microsoft is building out its architecture in a measured way and as such contains fewer surprises,” Ben Barringer, global head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said on Thursday. “Alphabet, by contrast, saw its share price hit after hours as a result of a fairly messy set of results and a poorly handled earnings call” . Alphabet’s biggest source of revenue, search advertising, grew 12% in the September quarter to $63.35 billion, but missed analyst expectations, adding further pressure to the company’s shares. Philipp Schindler, Alphabet’s chief business officer, said the impact on the search business was partly because of lower monetization within the company’s AI Mode. He added that Alphabet is now “scaling” ads within its AI Overviews and AI Mode products, including in international markets. Google’s search business has faced headwinds from the rise of other AI chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude. People may be carrying out more search queries outside Google. Gemini, Google’s own AI chatbot, has failed to keep pace. “The problem for Google is it faces an innovator’s dilemma and doesn’t know whether to protect its core business or look to join the disruption. As such, Google has lost its edge with Gemini and is behind peers on agentic AI,” Barringer said. Google’s dominant market share in the search business, however, could ultimately give it a leg up over its peers, Rosenblatt Securities analyst Scott Devitt said. “I don’t think it’s a sea change,” Devitt told CNBC’s “Squawk on the Street” on Thursday. “If it’s a problem for Alphabet, it’s a problem for any consumer-facing AI agent or LLM as well. And so, it’s a problem that I think is ultimately going to be resolved. And when it does, Alphabet, with its 4 billion search customers that become AI customers, is in an enviable position.” - CNBC’s Robert Hum, Samantha Subin, Jordan Novet and Caleigh Keating contributed reporting. Microsoft Cloud revenue surpassed $63 billion with growth accelerating to 30% year over year, driven by strong demand across Azure and M365 commercial cloud. Q: Karl Keirstead (UBS) asked Amy Hood to unpack the key drivers behind the surprisingly strong Azure growth guidance of 49% to 50% in constant currency for Q2. A: CFO Amy Hood explained that Q1 benefited from significant platform-layer efficiency gains across GPUs, CPUs, and the app stack, which allowed Microsoft to allocate more capacity to Foundry. She noted that higher-than-expected token pricing for high-quality models also contributed. For Q2, the guidance relies on continuing these efficiency gains to offset some third-party supply delays that shifted to the second half of the fiscal year, while acknowledging potential variability from token pricing. Q: Adam Wood (Morgan Stanley) asked whether improving utilization and unit costs within Azure or the ability to monetize more layers (Fabric, Foundry, Copilot) will be the more important driver of returns on AI capacity investments. A: CEO Satya Nadella stated it is "all of the above," emphasizing that Microsoft manages one fungible pool of infrastructure. He explained that margin leverage will come from every layerfrom the Copilot stateful database (WorkIQ) to Foundry for multi-agent systems, Azure databases like PostgreSQL, and security via Agent 365 and Perceptioncompounding when worked across the entire stack. Q: Mark Moerdler (Bernstein) asked for color on the mix of enterprise versus digitally native customers driving AI strength in Azure, and what is driving the growth of the Azure AI platform. A: CEO Satya Nadella highlighted a shift toward broad enterprise adoption, citing examples like Unilever's automated order-taking and Rolls-Royce's supply chain management built on Foundry. He noted that enterprises are increasingly focused on building systems they can own, manage costs for, and secure, rather than chasing "shiny objects." A: CEO Satya Nadella described a dynamic toolbox for customers: they may start with a new frontier model, then use multiple frontier models via routers like Copilot Fusion for cost/performance optimization, and ultimately train their own models (open weights or MAI) using their own traces. He emphasized that Microsoft wants to provide a model system that delivers continuous value, allowing customers to switch between options based on pricing and needs rather than being locked into one approach. Q: Brent Thill (Jefferies) asked how Microsoft can sustain ~50% top-line growth alongside ~50% operating margins, and what operational improvements support this. A: CFO Amy Hood emphasized that revenue growth is the primary solution, starting at the top of the P&L. She noted that efficiency improvements are not just about cost reduction but about operational excellencedelivering the highest-quality unit at the lowest cost, which improves stability, security, and reliability. She also highlighted a focus on directing operating expenses toward building new products and ensuring security and quality. Q: Brad Reback (Stifel) asked whether the shift to consumption-based models for core M365 tools will unlock revenue quickly or require significant sales effort, similar to GitHub's transition. A: CEO Satya Nadella said the coding side (GitHub) will move faster because customers are already used to pay-as-you-go models, and tools like Copilot Fusion make credit usage more efficient. For M365 Copilot, Microsoft is driving value into the subscription (funded by IT for broad deployment) while offering consumption meters for additional needs. title: MSFT Stock Jumps Above $550 Ahead of Fiscal First-Quarter Earnings as Microsoft Spending Concerns Mount - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft stock jumped above $550 after the fiscal Q1 earnings report, as cloud growth drives earnings and revenue beat. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares have pulled back toward $525 after failing to establish a new record above $550. The reversal follows a rally supported by news of the company’s custom-chip development, but investors are now weighing the potential returns from Microsoft’s expanding infrastructure commitments against rising competitive and regulatory risks. The company reports fiscal first-quarter earnings today, October 28, putting its cloud business, profitability and capital expenditure plans under close scrutiny. Despite strong historical earnings growth, buyers need evidence that Microsoft’s investment strategy can deliver sustainable returns without placing excessive pressure on cash generation. Microsoft reported net income of $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share, for the quarter, representing a 32% increase on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI. Revenue climbed to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier, while Wall Street had expected earnings of $4.27 per share and revenue of $90.6 billion, according to Bloomberg consensus estimates. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year over year, or 31% in constant currency. Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said results exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income and earnings per share, highlighting a strong start to the fiscal year. Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella said Microsoft was delivering greater computing capability, customer choice and cost efficiency, while focusing on security and helping organisations develop their own AI capabilities. Revenue from Microsoft’s Devices and Consumer segment fell 3% to $15.5 billion, reflecting weakness across several businesses. Search and advertising revenue, excluding traffic acquisition costs, increased 12%. However, Xbox content and services revenue declined 2%, or 1% in constant currency, while Windows OEM and Devices revenue dropped 22%. The contrasting results highlight continued cloud strength alongside weaker demand in parts of Microsoft’s consumer and hardware businesses. Microsoft’s financial performance remains robust. Fiscal 2026 revenue increased 18% to $331.8 billion, while net income climbed 31% to $133.7 billion. However, the cost of supporting its cloud and computing expansion is becoming increasingly important to investors. Capital expenditure reached $41 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter, with approximately two-thirds directed toward shorter-lived CPUs and GPUs. Operating cash flow totalled $55.4 billion, while free cash flow stood at $19.6 billion. Capital expenditure is expected to remain above $50 billion per quarter during fiscal 2027. These commitments raise questions about how quickly Microsoft’s revenue can expand to justify the spending. Even with strong demand, the company must demonstrate that its infrastructure investments can generate attractive returns rather than simply increasing operating capacity at considerable cost. Microsoft is developing its Maia 300 processor to improve computing efficiency and reduce reliance on external chip suppliers. The processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver up to seven times the rack-scale throughput of Maia 200. Custom silicon could eventually help Microsoft control computing costs, although development, deployment and infrastructure expansion require substantial upfront investment. The company has also reportedly discussed leasing computing capacity from SpaceX, according to The Information, although the current status of those talks remains unclear. SpaceX expects to finish 2026 with slightly more than 2 gigawatts of computing capacity and aims to expand to between 5 GW and 10 GW next year. Microsoft’s continued capacity constraints highlight the scale of the challenge, even as spending accelerates. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months, climb above $550 earlier this week but slipped below $530 again. The price slip tested the 20 daily SMA in gray in September which has been acting as support. The $550 area represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MAFT buyers gave up at this zone. Microsoft’s stock has undergone a notable repricing in recent months, signaling a broader reset in how investors are assessing mega-cap technology leaders. After peaking above $555 in October 2025, shares retreated sharply, and despite the revival in 2026, buyers haven’t been able to break above that level. The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has concluded an investigation launched in May 2026 into Microsoft’s software business, including Word, Excel and Teams. The watchdog believes Microsoft should receive a strategic market status designation, potentially allowing greater regulatory scrutiny and targeted interventions. The CMA has raised concerns about the difficulty customers may face when switching providers, Microsoft’s position among approximately 20 million UK users and the competitive implications of its Copilot offering. The proposed designation does not establish wrongdoing. However, additional oversight could increase compliance costs and place restrictions on pricing, licensing or product-bundling strategies. Microsoft also faces intensifying competition from Google Workspace as businesses reassess Microsoft 365 pricing and bundled features. Maintaining its position in productivity software will require continued innovation while protecting margins. Meanwhile, the company is restructuring its gaming division, with approximately 3,200 job reductions planned during fiscal 2027, including 1,600 immediate cuts. The reductions reflect efforts to improve efficiency as Microsoft manages costs across its broader operations.

title: Microsoft stock jumps 4% as cloud growth drives earnings and revenue beat - CNBC
content:
Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business. Here’s how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus: Microsoft’s revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement, with Azure now its biggest single business. The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported  $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion. With respect to guidance, Microsoft called for $96 billion to $97.1 billion in fiscal second-quarter revenue, which works out to 18.8% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $95.60 billion in revenue. For Azure, Microsoft’s finance chief, Amy Hood, said on a conference call with analysts that she anticipates 49% to 50% growth at constant currency for the fiscal second quarter, compared with the 45.1% StreetAccount consensus. “We still have demand that exceeds supply,” she said. During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases. “Some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed,” Hood said. Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft’s prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue. Hood said the company is aiming at over $50 billion in fiscal second-quarter capital expenditures and finance leases, above the StreetAccount consensus of $53.10 billion, with $170 billion for all of calendar 2027 because of the capacity issues. “In the second half of the fiscal year, we currently expect capex spend to accelerate primarily from CPUs, inclusive of higher memory and storage costs, and GPUs, as well as the 3P capacity deliveries that shifted to H2,” she said. The delays have to do with GPU-as-a-service providers, she said. Free cash flow for the fiscal first quarter declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time. Microsoft will continue to generate free cash flow through the 2027 fiscal year, but the company will access additional sources of funding when it’s attractive to do so, Hood said. “We’re fortunate to have access in the debt markets, given where our rates ratings are, and sort of we haven’t been able to — we haven’t yet, I would say, tapped that,” she said. “And then, of course, there’s other options.” Microsoft’s net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI. For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter, despite the delays from third-party providers. Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%. Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.  For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses. In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services. The number of people using the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant is up 50% from last quarter, CEO Satya Nadella said on the call. The company did not disclose the number of paid seats. The recently announced high-end Microsoft 365 E7 productivity bundle now has millions of seats, Hood said. Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers. Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand. As of Wednesday’s close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period. During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs, and followed up by announcing on Monday that it’s offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. We came across a bullish thesis on Amazon.com, Inc. on Quality Stocks | GARP Investment Research's Substack. Since the thesis was published on August 26th, AMZN shares have edged lower amid concerns that heavy AI infrastructure spending could pressure near-term cash flow, creating a short-term headwind while strong AWS growth supports the long-term case. In this article, we will summarize the bulls' thesis on AMZN. Amazon.com, Inc.'s share was trading at $253.10 as of October 27th 2026. AMZN's trailing and forward P/E were 20.04 and 23.10 respectively according to Yahoo Finance. This isn't the first time we see a technology company pitched as a great investment. AMZN shares gained 9.90% over the last 12 months. Comparable stocks like Alphabet gained 16.76% during the same period. Why are technology stocks rising, and does AMZN's slower climb leave room for it to catch up? In July, we published an article about the 12 Best Dow Stocks to Invest In Right Now and AMZN ranked 1st in that article. AMZN has gained modestly since then, keeping the bullish call in positive territory but giving investors little to celebrate so far. This article explains why hedge funds were bullish on AMZN. Before getting into our analysis, let's take a look at the business and why some investors like the stock so much. Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) operates one of the largest consumer, cloud computing, advertising, and logistics ecosystems in the world. Its investment case increasingly depends on AWS, artificial intelligence infrastructure, advertising, and a shift toward higher-margin businesses rather than traditional e-commerce. Sales growth has been strong and steady, rising 12% in 2024 and an estimated 15% in 2025, with a similar pace expected in 2026 as Amazon.com, Inc. moves toward $1 trillion in annual revenue. Read More: 15 AI Stocks That Are Quietly Making Investors Rich Read More: Undervalued AI Stock Poised For Massive Gains: 10000% Upside Potential AWS alone generated $45.6 billion in operating income in 2025, underlining how central cloud computing has become to the company's profits. The stock trades around 21 times earnings at $262 per share, a multiple that rises closer to 30 times once one-time, non-operating gains are stripped out — a reminder that investors are really paying for future AWS growth, AI monetization, and margin improvement rather than today's reported earnings. The bullish case rests on several growth engines reinforcing one another. Higher-margin segments such as AWS, advertising, third-party seller services, and subscriptions are letting profits grow faster than overall sales. Online retail is still the biggest source of revenue for Amazon.com, Inc., but advertising and third-party services are more profitable, while AWS remains both the company's main earnings driver and its gateway into the AI boom. As more companies increase spending on AI infrastructure, AWS stands to benefit from rising demand for computing power, storage, databases, and AI tools such as Amazon Bedrock, opening up a fresh growth cycle for the business. The AI ambitions of Amazon.com, Inc. go beyond AWS. The company is also applying artificial intelligence to warehouse automation, logistics, advertising targeting, product recommendations, and tools that help third-party sellers run their businesses more efficiently. AWS's growth rate has accelerated sharply, from 18% to 35%, a sign that Amazon.com, Inc. remains competitive even as Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud post faster growth of their own. Even so, the company still has to prove that its heavy AI investments will generate strong returns and turn into durable earnings growth (see whether Amazon's custom AI chips can outpace its capital spending). Operating leverage is a key part of the investment case, as Amazon.com, Inc. shifts toward more profitable businesses and becomes more efficient across its operations. Management expects capital spending of around $200 billion in 2026, mostly for AI infrastructure, data centers, and chips — spending large enough to push free cash flow into negative territory. Bulls see this as growth investment rather than routine maintenance spending, but it also means Amazon.com, Inc. needs strong AWS growth and sustained AI demand to justify spending at this scale over the coming years. The revenue mix of Amazon.com, Inc. is steadily shifting toward higher-value services. Advertising, third-party seller services, subscriptions, and AWS are becoming a larger part of the business relative to lower-margin first-party retail. This shift matters because it lets profits grow faster than revenue as these segments gain a bigger share of the overall mix. Based on this trajectory, expected returns work out to roughly 12.1% annualized, driven by organic growth, expanding margins, and an overall improvement in business quality. On valuation, the stock already reflects a good deal of optimism. A base-case fair value estimate puts shares of Amazon.com, Inc. around $251, with a bull-case scenario reaching $305 if revenue growth and operating margins come in stronger than expected. At current levels, the stock doesn't look dramatically overvalued, but it also doesn't offer much of a safety cushion, since investors are already paying up for faster AWS growth, AI-driven gains, and improving profitability. If AI spending falls short of expectations, AWS growth slows, or operating leverage disappoints, the premium built into the stock could come under pressure. The biggest risk to this thesis is that AI demand may stay concentrated among a small number of large customers, even as it requires enormous upfront investment. The $200 billion capital spending plan of Amazon.com, Inc. could pay off handsomely if cloud demand keeps accelerating, but weaker AI adoption, pricing pressure, or slower monetization could leave the company with high infrastructure costs and limited profit growth. Competition across cloud computing, advertising, retail, logistics, and AI — along with regulatory scrutiny — adds further uncertainty to the long-term picture. Another risk for the stock is disruption to the systems that support AWS and Amazon's wider operations. Customers rely on these services to keep applications, payments, and business processes running, making reliability central to the cloud franchise. Amazon warns that system failures or security incidents can interrupt services, cause data loss, and expose it to liability. A prolonged outage could disrupt customers and require costly remediation. Repeated incidents could also weaken confidence and make businesses more cautious about placing additional workloads on AWS. These pressures could hurt growth and profitability even if demand for AI computing remains strong. In our opinion, Amazon's premium valuation becomes harder to defend if reliability problems undermine its main earnings engine. Hedge fund positioning shows a strong signal for Amazon.com, Inc. As per our database, 369 hedge fund portfolios held the stock at the end of the second quarter, up from 353 in the previous quarter. This steady rise in institutional ownership suggests hedge funds remained constructive on Amazon.com, Inc.'s AWS growth, AI opportunity, advertising business, and long-term margin expansion potential. By comparison, Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) was held by 273 hedge fund portfolios, down from 282, Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) was held by 195 hedge funds, down from 201, and Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) was held by 119 hedge funds, up from 115. The rise in ownership of Amazon.com, Inc. and Oracle Corporation, against declines for Microsoft Corporation and Alphabet Inc., points to relatively stronger institutional conviction toward Amazon.com, Inc. during the period, even as funds continue weighing its premium valuation and heavy AI spending against its long-term growth potential. Short interest data also paints a fairly calm picture for Amazon.com, Inc. relative to its peers. About 0.88% of Amazon.com, Inc.'s float is sold short, slightly higher than Microsoft Corporation at 0.82%, but below Alphabet Inc. at 1.37% and well below Oracle Corporation at 2.60%. This suggests Amazon.com, Inc. is drawing similarly limited skepticism to Microsoft Corporation, while bearish bets remain less aggressive than those against Alphabet Inc. and Oracle Corporation, even as investors weigh its valuation and capital spending. AMZN's forward P/E is 23.10x. Microsoft Corporation, Oracle Corporation, and Alphabet Inc. trade at forward P/Es of 26.88x, 15.54x, and 20.24x, respectively. AMZN's own forward P/E was 22.96x on December 31, 2025, making its current valuation approximately 0.6% higher. We believe the current valuation reflects expectations for AWS growth, advertising expansion, and improving margins, balanced against concerns about heavy AI spending and uncertain investment returns. However, the valuation appears reasonable rather than deeply discounted, as Amazon trades below Microsoft but above Oracle and Alphabet. AWS generated $45.6 billion in operating income in 2025, while Amazon's approximately $200 billion capital spending plan for 2026 underscores how much future growth depends on earning adequate returns from new infrastructure. We believe AMZN can justify its current valuation if higher-margin businesses sustain earnings growth while absorbing rising depreciation and financing costs. If Amazon maintains its cloud momentum and successfully turns AI investment into lasting profits and cash flow, the current valuation could offer a reasonable entry point despite the risks surrounding its infrastructure expansion. Previously, we covered a bullish thesis on Amazon.com, Inc. (AMZN) by FluentInQuality in May 2025, which highlighted AWS growth, logistics infrastructure, Prime ecosystem, advertising strength, and Amazon's five interconnected category leaders. AMZN's stock price has appreciated by approximately 23.16% since our coverage. We believe AMZN is a reasonable long-term investment if AWS and other higher-margin businesses turn its AI spending into sustained earnings and cash flow, though the current valuation leaves limited room for execution missteps.
